text: An undercover officer is a professional liar, which makes her a poor guest in any community that runs on trust. Emily Eden works homicide in New York, and a murder she cannot read from outside puts her inside a world with unwritten law and unspoken power, where her ordinary instruments — pressure, deception, the badge in her pocket — are the crudest things in the room. Lumet had been filming the city's precincts and courtrooms for decades, and what interests him here is friction: how an investigation proceeds when the usual leverage does not apply, when questions have to be asked sideways, when the pace of the case has to match the pace of a household. It carries a place on the European Film Awards Best Film list, an odd address for a New York police picture. Under the procedure is a woman discovering that her method is itself the trespass.

Cumberland, 1348: the plague has not reached the village yet, and a nine-year-old keeps dreaming the same handful of images. A lake with a coffin floating on it. A white church, an iron cross, a glove falling, a torch dropping down a shaft with no bottom. His brother reads the dream as instruction, and a few men set out to dig toward a distant cathedral and raise the cross there as an offering. Ward takes the belief at its word — nobody in the party argues with a vision, so the doubt has to arrive from the far end of the tunnel, where the shaft lets them out into a century they have no words for. Ninety-two minutes, most of them underground or in the dark, cut and lit with the care that took the AACTA award for cinematography. The logic is medieval and consistent: a plague is a judgment, a dream is a map, and the sane response to catastrophe is to climb down.

A guest arrives for the weekend, and a teenage girl begins measuring her father against him. The trip is to the Adriatic; the visitor is rich, foreign, an old friend of the family; and the daughter's calculation is closer to administration than to romance — replace one man's authority with another's, on the theory that the new one might be lighter to carry. Kusijanović explains almost nothing. The father's temper registers in the way the others in a room arrange themselves around it, and the mother's silences keep their own accounts. Ninety-five minutes, one household, a few days of coastline and company in Croatian, with the sea always available as an argument for leaving. What the film is really watching is the moment a child works out that the adults around her are negotiable.

Josie Alibrandi is seventeen, and the question of where she fits has stopped being a mood and become a practical problem. Kate Woods treats that as comedy at least as often as grievance, the two being frequently the same joke told from a different chair. The adaptation took the AACTA award for adapted screenplay, and the writing shows in the traffic: mothers and grandmothers and boys all talking across one another while Josie tries to hold a position long enough to defend it. A hundred and three minutes, Australian, kept close to the ground — no discovery arrives without a kitchen argument attached to it. Its real subject is the year a girl stops being the youngest person in the room and starts being answerable, which turns out to be a series of conversations she would rather not have.

One alley in Mexico City, and inside it several futures being planned at cross purposes. Fons spends a hundred and forty minutes with people who cannot quite afford their own plans: a bar owner's son set on the United States, a barber in love with a neighbour he has not thought to ask, a woman past the age her street considers marriageable and out of patience with that arithmetic. None of this is subplot. The length exists so that each life can be watched at its own speed, and so that a decision taken on one side of the alley arrives as weather on the other. Mexico sent it to the Academy Awards as its submission. What the film does is hold a neighbourhood still long enough to show how little privacy poverty leaves for wanting things, and how fast a want becomes everyone's business.

Canned food, a window with the neighbours in it, and a phone call describing a social life that does not exist. Laura is a journalist in Mexico City who files from home, so the apartment is both her office and the full extent of her week. Rowe builds the film out of repetition — the same meals, the same view, the same lies told to her mother and her brother Raul — and then lets Arturo in, a man she brings back the way she brings back others and then keeps bringing back. What the two of them arrange is not romance, and the film declines to soften it into one. A date is coming: the anniversary of her father's death, which she discusses with nobody. Ninety-four minutes in Spanish, and the discipline is in the withholding — the camera stays where Laura's life is, which is a few rooms and a very short list of people.

Paula comes back to Paris with a cat, no money, and a run of doors closing in front of her. The film moves at the speed of practical problems — a bed for tonight, work that starts tomorrow, someone who might be persuaded — and Serraille never lets any of it accumulate into a lesson. Paula talks constantly. She is funny when she intends to be and funnier when she does not, and her insistence on getting through this with style is filmed as a working strategy rather than a character flaw. Ninety-seven minutes, present-day Paris seen from the height of someone consulting a bus map. The audience award at IFFR suggests the experience: the pleasure is her company, and the one real generosity is that the film refuses to decide in advance whether she will be all right.

Malcolm was fired for building his own tram, which explains both what he can do and why he cannot keep a job. He has an engineer's hands and no idea how to be in a room with another person, so when a lodger just out of prison moves in to help with the bills, the two competencies in the house turn out to fit together in a way neither man planned. Tass films the machines with attention, and the comedy depends on it: the things Malcolm builds work on screen, plainly, before anyone puts them to illegal use. Eighty-six minutes, Australian, built as a heist assembled out of hobbies. What keeps it from settling into whimsy is that the shyness is never treated as a condition to be cured — the same wiring that makes him useless at conversation makes him exact with anything that has moving parts.

One girl has money and no friends; the other has neither, and a claim that changes the rate of exchange between them. Mexico City, 1965: Flavia is wealthy, unattended and grateful for company, while Veronica says she is a witch and there is no adult nearby with any interest in checking. What follows is a fantasy sustained by two people, in which belief has to be paid for — errands, secrets, small cruelties, each demanded as evidence of loyalty. Taboada keeps the pressure entirely between the girls, and ninety minutes is exactly long enough for a game to harden into an arrangement. The Ariel for best picture went to it, which is not where horror usually ends up. The mechanism is the frightening part: no spell is required once one child has convinced another that she is dangerous.

A bride breaks her leg getting out of a locked toilet stall at her own wedding. The Caribbean honeymoon is off, and Keren starts her marriage unable to walk. Two other women are working that reception. Batya carries trays, and later finds a small child at the beach with nobody attached to her. Joy is there as an employer's companion, speaks English in a city conducting itself in Hebrew, and has a son back in the Philippines she can reach only at a distance. Geffen keeps the three of them in the same Tel Aviv without insisting they mean anything to one another; they share rooms because of work, not fate. Eighty-two minutes, and the method is to hold the camera on the practical surface — trays, crutches, phone calls — and let what each of them is carrying show through it.

Three men who have never met are in the same restaurant, and by the time they leave the city has decided they are working together. None of them decided anything. Trivisa runs on that rumour: three notorious Hong Kong thieves, each separately occupied with his own difficulties, find that a story about an alliance travels faster than any of them can correct it, and that the Handover is coming whether or not their affairs are in order. Ninety-six minutes for three parallel careers is tight, and the compression is the point — nobody here has the leisure to reconsider. What is unusual is how unglamorous the crime is made to look: supply problems, unreliable partners, a trade getting harder to practise in a city about to be administered by someone else.

Magdalena's son left for the border and never arrived, so she goes north herself to find out where he stopped. Valadez films the search as a passage through country where information is the scarcest thing available: names nobody will say aloud, routes that no longer run, an office that hands back a form. On the way she falls in with Miguel, recently deported from the other side and travelling home to his own mother — two searches pointed in opposite directions, sharing a road for a while. Ninety-five minutes, and the dread is built out of landscape and low light rather than incident; the thriller machinery is there, slowed almost to stillness. It took the Golden Alexander. What the film understands is that a disappearance is not one event but a condition a family has to keep re-entering, counter by counter, to get any answer at all.
